name: Education, Talent & Future of Work
label: SECTOR EXPLORATION PACK | WORKSHOP 1
referenceMarket: United States (Miami/Florida as a reference case; national-scope ideas are welcome)
intro: This Pack gives you a common starting point: vocabulary, structure and verified figures. It does not define the problem, customer or solution. That is your job.
definition: Businesses and institutions that educate, train, certify, match and manage people across their careers, from college to workforce reskilling, plus the technology and services that power them.
inside: Higher education and alternative credentials (certificates, bootcamps, apprenticeships)
Edtech and B2B services to schools and employers
outside: Building and operating campuses as real estate
Government programs themselves (they can be customers or partners)

players.howMoney: Tuition and fees, federal and state aid, research funding; online programs often run with an external partner on revenue share.
players.examples: Miami Dade College, FIU, UF, MIU.

players.howMoney: Subscriptions, per-course fees, paid certificates, and B2B licenses sold to employers and universities.
Tuition, employer-paid placement fees, sometimes income-share agreements. Outcomes-based credibility.
SaaS subscription per learner or employee, content licensing, implementation services.
Subscriptions, pay-per-post or pay-per-click, success fees on hires, premium candidate search.
Markup on hourly pay, placement fees, marketplace take rate on freelance work.
SaaS per employee per month, payroll processing and compliance fees, employer-of-record fees for global hiring.
Freemium subscriptions, tutoring by the hour, institutional licenses, student financing products.

playersNote: Illustrative map, not exhaustive. Examples are well-known players to help you recognize each model, not a recommendation to copy them.

valueChain.note: One possible lens. The chain changes by segment (higher education, corporate training, recruiting, HR software). Map the one that fits your area of interest and decide where value is created and captured.

figuresNote: Some figures are preliminary or estimates. Always check the latest release and cite the source and year in your own work.
challenge: The U.S. labor market is changing: hiring is slow, AI is reshaping the skills employers need, and learners and companies struggle to link education to real job outcomes, while the cost of learning and student debt weigh on households. Identify one specific, evidence-backed friction experienced by a clearly defined customer (a learner, a worker, an employer or an institution) in the U.S., and show why it is worth solving now. Choose an initial launch market (for example Miami/Florida or another U.S. region) and justify your choice with data.
pestelNote: Sprint 1, PESTEL: each team member takes one dimension. The figures above are a starting point only; look for what is changing and who it affects.

sprint2Questions.question: Who pays for learning and who benefits (learner, employer, government, institution)? Who holds the trust and the data?
At which step of the talent journey do learners or employers lose time, money or confidence? Who captures the margin?
What is still manual, opaque or slow in learning, hiring or onboarding? What evidence shows it matters (surveys, outcomes, costs)?
How is the problem solved today, and by whom? Which solutions fail to prove outcomes for their customer?
Which group is most affected: early-career workers, career changers, adult learners, small employers, institutions? How large is it?
Who pays in your idea (learner, employer, institution, government) and why? How long is the sales cycle, and how do you prove results?

glossary.def: New skills for a current role (reskilling: for a new role)
Short, verifiable certificate for a specific skill
Federal student aid programs; access depends on accreditation
Learning management system: software to deliver training
Applicant tracking system: software to manage hiring
Paid, structured on-the-job training with instruction
Income-share agreement: learner pays a share of future income
Total recruiting cost divided by the number of hires
Per employee per month: common SaaS pricing in HR software
Share of enrolled learners who finish a program or course
